title: Bronchiolitis
subject: paediatrics
summary: Clinical diagnosis in children under 2 years (peak 3 to 6 months) after a coryzal prodrome. Care is supportive: oxygen only if SpO2 stays below 90% (below 92% under 6 weeks or with comorbidity), NG or IV fluids for poor intake, and no salbutamol, steroids, adrenaline, hypertonic saline or antibiotics (NICE NG9 2021, AAP 2014).

sections.title: Diagnose clinically
items: Child under 2 years (most in the first year, peak 3 to 6 months) with coryza for 1 to 3 days followed by persistent cough, tachypnoea or chest recession, and wheeze or crackles.
Fever occurs in about 30% (usually below 39 °C). Symptoms peak at day 3 to 5, poor feeding often starts then, and cough may last up to 3 weeks.
Young infants, especially under 6 weeks, may present with apnoea alone.
Think of pneumonia with fever above 39 °C or persistent focal crackles, and of viral-induced wheeze or asthma in older infants with recurrent wheeze without crackles or atopy.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Measure SpO2 in every child with suspected bronchiolitis using a correctly placed paediatric probe; oximeters can overestimate saturation in darker skin.
Do not routinely do blood tests, blood gases, chest X-ray or viral swabs; X-ray changes mimic pneumonia and lead to unnecessary antibiotics.
Consider capillary blood gas in severe worsening distress (oxygen above 50%) or impending respiratory failure, and a chest X-ray if intensive care is being planned.

sections.title: Refer or admit
items: Emergency referral: apnoea, child looks seriously unwell, severe distress (grunting, marked recession or respiratory rate over 70/min) or central cyanosis.

Admit if persistent SpO2 in air below 90% (age 6 weeks or more) or below 92% (under 6 weeks or with underlying disease), intake 50 to 75% of normal or clinical dehydration, apnoea, or persisting severe distress.

Lower threshold with risk factors: chronic lung disease, haemodynamically significant heart disease, age under 3 months, prematurity (especially below 32 weeks), neuromuscular disease, immunodeficiency, and social or distance barriers to care.

sections.title: Supportive treatment
items: Oxygen only if SpO2 is persistently below 90% (6 weeks or older) or below 92% (under 6 weeks or comorbidity). AAP 2014 likewise allows no oxygen at 90% or above. Brief dips are not a reason to start oxygen.

If SpO2 stays below 90% with no improvement after about 2 hours of low-flow oxygen, consider high-flow nasal cannula. Consider CPAP for impending respiratory failure (exhaustion, recurrent apnoea, failing saturation despite oxygen).

Fluids: NG or orogastric feeds if oral intake is inadequate; IV isotonic fluid with glucose only if NG feeds are not tolerated or respiratory failure is impending. Some units start NG or IV fluids at two-thirds maintenance because of ADH excess.
Suction: not routine; superficial nasal suction if secretions cause distress or feeding difficulty, and always in infants presenting with apnoea.

Do not use salbutamol, ipratropium, nebulised adrenaline, oral or inhaled corticosteroids, montelukast, nebulised hypertonic saline or antibiotics. No chest physiotherapy unless there is a relevant comorbidity such as spinal muscular atrophy.

sections.title: Monitoring and escalation
items: Observe respiratory rate, work of breathing, SpO2, apnoea, feeding and hydration; expect the worst around day 3 to 5 of illness.
Trial off oxygen regularly and stop continuous oximetry once off oxygen and improving.
Call PICU or retrieval for recurrent apnoea, exhaustion or reduced effort, rising oxygen need (above 50% on high flow), or hypercapnic respiratory failure.

sections.title: Discharge and advice
items: Discharge when clinically stable, taking adequate oral fluids, and SpO2 in air has stayed above 90% (above 92% under 6 weeks or with comorbidity) for 4 hours including a period of sleep.

Tell carers to return for worsening breathing (grunting, flaring, marked recession), intake 50 to 75% of normal or no wet nappy for 12 hours, apnoea or cyanosis, or exhaustion. Advise no smoking in the home.
Prevention for high-risk infants (preterm, chronic lung disease, significant heart disease): RSV monoclonal antibody or maternal RSV vaccination according to national availability and policy.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating with bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics because of wheeze or fever.
Admitting or keeping children in hospital only for brief desaturations or a saturation target in the mid to high 90s.
Missing serious bacterial infection in febrile infants under 3 months, or heart failure in a wheezy infant with a murmur or hepatomegaly.

drugs.name: Oxygen (nasal prongs or high-flow nasal cannula)
drugs.dose: Start only if SpO2 persistently below 90% (below 92% under 6 weeks or with comorbidity); titrate to 90% or above
drugs.notes: Trial off regularly; high flow if no improvement after about 2 hours of low-flow oxygen.

drugs.name: Isotonic IV fluid with glucose (for example 0.9% saline with 5% dextrose)
drugs.dose: Only if NG or orogastric feeds are not tolerated; many units give two-thirds of maintenance
drugs.notes: Monitor sodium; risk of hyponatraemia from ADH excess.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg orally every 4 to 6 hours (max 60 mg/kg/day)
drugs.notes: For discomfort or fever; no other routine medicines.
